title: Eastern US tree growth and survival did not change on average with the 2000-2025 sulfur deposition decrease in 15 FIA states, but red spruce sites grew faster where sulfur decreased most
abstract: Question: when total sulfur (S) deposition decreased by about 85% in 2000-2025, did eastern US trees grow faster and die less by the amount that spatial deposition relations predict? Data: USDA FIA annual inventory remeasurements in 15 states (NH to TN; 12,739 plots, 327,707 trees >= 12.7 cm DBH, 617,033 growth and 718,389 mortality intervals), NADP/EPA TDep total S and N grids 2000-2024, nClimGrid weather. Method: spatial models of first intervals (Horn-type) and within-tree models with tree and state-by-year fixed effects, so that the S slope comes from plots with different S decreases in the same state and year; per-species models for 25 species; weather terms as positive controls. Results: the pooled within-tree S slope was -0.0003 of species-mean growth per kg S/ha/yr (95% CI -0.0072 to +0.0067). For the mean plot decrease of 6.2 kg this gives +0.2% growth (CI -4.2% to +4.5%; -9.6% to +9.9% with state clusters). Mortality also had no clear S slope. The pooled spatial S slopes were near zero or positive, so no growth gain was predicted. Precipitation (+2.9% growth per 100 mm) and temperature (+0.31%/yr mortality per 1 C) were detected. Red spruce was the one species where spatial (-0.139, SE 0.089) and within-tree (-0.156, SE 0.036) S slopes agreed: it grew faster where S decreased most. Other conifers had smaller negative slopes (all conifers -0.027, SE 0.011; hardwoods +0.001). Hardwoods on red spruce plots had the same negative slope (-0.060, SE 0.016), so the response belongs more to spruce-fir sites than to the species. Across 25 species the spatial slope did not predict the temporal slope without red spruce (Spearman 0.13). Limitations: no ozone term; deposition before 2000 not available; S and N correlate (0.78); the 2003 red spruce winter injury falls in early intervals; perturbed plot coordinates; heterogeneity tests are exploratory.
